parts.move: state the photon energy relation and the meaning of each symbol
parts.prompt: State the equation relating photon energy to frequency, and define each symbol.
scheme: h is Planck's constant, f is the frequency
parts.answer: A photon's energy is E = hf = hc/λ, where h is Planck's constant and f is the frequency.

parts.move: state the electronvolt and its joule equivalence
parts.prompt: Define the electronvolt and state its value in joules.
scheme: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron through 1 V
parts.answer: One electronvolt is the energy an electron gains accelerating through 1 V, equal to 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

parts.move: explain the threshold frequency from the one-photon energy balance
parts.prompt: Explain, in terms of photons, why no electrons are emitted below a metal's threshold frequency regardless of intensity.
scheme: A photon must supply at least the work function to free an electron
Below threshold hf < φ so no single photon can liberate an electron
Extra intensity adds photons but not per-photon energy
parts.answer: Emission needs hf ≥ φ. Below the threshold frequency each photon carries less than the work function, so no electron is freed however intense the light, because one electron absorbs one photon.

parts.move: explain why only the fastest electrons have the maximum kinetic energy
parts.prompt: Explain why emitted photoelectrons have a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum value.
scheme: KEmax = hf − φ is the energy left after escape
Electrons from deeper in the metal lose extra energy, so they emerge slower
parts.answer: KEmax = hf − φ is the surplus after the least-bound surface electron escapes; electrons from below lose further energy on the way out, so most emerge with less than the maximum.

parts.move: apply E = hf to a frequency change and take the difference in maximum kinetic energy
parts.prompt: Light on a metal changes from 6.0×10¹⁴ Hz to 8.0×10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the increase in the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s)
parts.answer: Raising the frequency by 2.0×10¹⁴ Hz adds hΔf = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ × 2.0×10¹⁴ = 1.33×10⁻¹⁹ J to the maximum kinetic energy.

parts.move: convert a wavelength to photon energy with E = hc/λ
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of a 500 nm photon in joules. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹)

parts.move: separate photon energy (frequency) from photon rate (intensity)
parts.prompt: A student doubles the intensity of above-threshold light and expects the fastest electrons to double in kinetic energy. Explain the error and predict what changes.
scheme: Intensity changes the number of photons per second, not each photon's energy
Photon energy depends only on frequency, so KEmax is unchanged by intensity
parts.answer: Brighter light sends more photons each second, releasing more electrons, but each photon's energy hf is unchanged, so the maximum kinetic energy does not rise.

parts.move: reject the idea that every incident photon ejects an electron
parts.prompt: A student claims every photon above the threshold frequency ejects an electron. Explain why emission efficiency is below 100%.
scheme: Above threshold not every photon causes emission; some pass through or miss electrons
Intensity above threshold raises the rate but the efficiency is below 100%
parts.answer: Even above the threshold, only a fraction of photons eject electrons; increasing intensity raises the emission rate proportionally but never makes every photon successful.

parts.move: transfer the photon-energy model to an LED to estimate Planck's constant
parts.prompt: An LED emits 620 nm light when electrons cross a 1.9 V junction. Estimate Planck's constant from these values. (e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C, c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹)
parts.answer: Setting eV = hc/λ gives h = eVλ/c = (1.60×10⁻¹⁹ × 1.9 × 620×10⁻⁹)/(3.0×10⁸) ≈ 6.3×10⁻³⁴ J s.

parts.move: apply photon energy to a power budget to find photons per second
parts.prompt: A 2.0 W beam of 620 nm light falls on a surface. Calculate how many photons arrive per second. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹)
scheme: Energy per photon E = hc/λ = 3.21e-19 J (620 nm)
parts.answer: Each 620 nm photon carries 3.21×10⁻¹⁹ J, so a 2.0 W beam delivers 2.0/3.21×10⁻¹⁹ = 6.2×10¹⁸ photons each second.

parts.move: combine the photoelectric balance with eVs = KEmax to find the stopping potential
parts.prompt: Light of frequency 1.0×10¹⁵ Hz falls on a metal of work function 3.0×10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the stopping potential. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C)
parts.answer: KEmax = hf − φ = 6.63×10⁻¹⁹ − 3.0×10⁻¹⁹ = 3.63×10⁻¹⁹ J. The stopping potential is Vs = KEmax/e = 3.63×10⁻¹⁹/1.60×10⁻¹⁹ = 2.3 V.

parts.move: link a level difference to a photon energy then to its wavelength
parts.prompt: An atomic transition releases 3.0 eV. Calculate the wavelength of the emitted photon. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J)
scheme: Photon energy = level difference = 3.0 eV = 4.80e-19 J
parts.answer: A 3.0 eV transition emits a 4.80×10⁻¹⁹ J photon; λ = hc/E = (6.63×10⁻³⁴×3.0×10⁸)/4.80×10⁻¹⁹ = 4.1×10⁻⁷ m, about 414 nm.
